verdict: OK to lend in Khurja ceramics, but only to gas-contract-backed units with verified kiln utilisation; avoid units still running on spot LPG or with cold kilns.
title: Khurja Ceramic Tiles, Sanitaryware & Glass: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
The kiln is the whole business; if it is cold, nothing converts. So when a proposal lands, check the gas supply contract and the last three months of kiln running days before you look at anything else. ## Where value and cash sit
**Fuel is the swing cost, and it has broken: piped gas that hovered around Rs 49 per kg before the West Asia conflict shot to Rs 120 per kg at peak and sits near Rs 90 per kg now [1].** That is the pricing-power test. A unit that cannot pass this through is losing money on every firing. Kajaria's Q1 shows the other side: revenue up 20% on tile realisations up 11% and bathware up 16%, with margins expanding 266 basis points [5][6]. So when a proposal lands, ask for the last six months' gas bills and selling prices side by side; if realisations have not moved with gas, ask how the gap is funded. The official pack is more constructive: UP GST collections up 14.2% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1%, and IIP for NIC 23 output up 11.4% YoY [D]. Peer results confirm demand is intact but gas-constrained: Somany grew revenue 6% at an 11.4% EBITDA margin in Q4 FY26 [7]. The gap between cluster distress and national demand is exactly where selection matters. ## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue units with a piped-gas connection, ODOP export orders, and a product mix shifting to higher-realisation bathware and tiles; the ODOP push is opening global markets for Khurja pottery [2][3].** Avoid pure spot-LPG crockery units with no export order book and no price-pass-through. Structure as working capital against verified gas bills and order confirmations, with a covenant that kiln running days do not fall below a stated floor. Take monthly: gas consumption and per-kg rate, kiln running days, sales realisation per unit, and debtor ageing. Kajaria's own rating history shows the safe shape: negligible long-term debt, working capital lines used only for a few months, and large cash buffers [9][11]. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch for a unit drawing term debt to fund fuel, which converts a working-capital shock into a solvency problem.** ICRA flags exactly this: debt-funded capex or a stretched working capital cycle weakening liquidity leads to rating pressure [10]. If monthly gas rate crosses the peak seen in the local report and realisations stay flat, stop fresh limits and ask for the order book. If kiln running days drop below the covenant floor, move to stock and receivable review.
watch: Gas rate and kiln running days (monthly)
rate above the peak cited locally with flat realisations -> freeze fresh limits
any term loan raised to fund fuel -> treat as solvency signal, escalate
order book falls below three months of sales -> reduce limit
turnover drop against prior quarter -> recheck kiln utilisation
